newsitem.title: GERMANY: F.O. Licht - Third estimate of world sugar balance.
newsitem.headline: F.O. Licht - Third estimate of world sugar balance.

text.p: THIRD ESTIMATE OF THE WORLD SUGAR BALANCE 1996/97
September/August (1000 tonnes, raw value)
previous
estimate*
Opening
Stocks in %

The world sugar balance has sprung no surprises over the past several months. We are now putting production in September/August 1996/97 at 123.2 million tonnes, compared with our initial estimate of 124.0 million tonnes and last year's figure of 125.9 million tones. Compared with our first estimate this is a reduction of just 0.6 per cent, meanwhile we have increased our estimate of consumption by less than 1 per cent. In such stable conditions it is hardly surprising that there has been a high degree of price stability.

Asia is the continent in which production is below earlier expectations. In all other areas output is about the same or in excess of the tonnages originally projected. After last year's big jump production in Asia is expected to fall by 9 per cent to 37.6 million tonnes. Several countries contributed to this but India was foremost with a drop from 17.9 million tonnes last season to 14.4 million tonnes.
Production in West Europe was higher than had been anticipated with the EU at 18 million tonnes, up 1.5 percent on our previous estimate and 1 million more than produced in 1995/96.

Production in West Europe outside the EU is now put at 2.7 million tonnes against 2.0 million last year. In East Europe production is a little higher than initially forecast but just shy of last year's figure of 9.71 million tonnes.
In Africa output is put at 8.6 million tonnes compared with last year's figure of 8.1 million tonnes. This increase largely reflects higher output in the South African Republic.
The picture for North and Central America is clouded by the lack of real knowledge from Cuba, although we know that for several reasons the crop has hit problems.

Estimating production in South America on a September/August basis poses special problems as in many cases this cuts across two crop years. Brazil is by far the largest producer in the continent and the 1996/97 crop plan for 1997/98 calls for an output of 13.48 million tonnes, tel quel, slightly below last year's plan of 13.68 million tonnes. Some in Brazil expect output to exceed this figure. In Oceania Australia continues its relentless rise in output but with latest cane production estimates expected to show a smaller rise on the year.

For some years there was a disappointing trend in world consumption but since 1994/95 the pattern has been reversed. In 1996/97 the increase is estimated to reach 2.7 per cent. Factors responsible for this change in trend include the fact that the decline in East Europe appears to have come to an end, the substitution process in the USA has almost come to a halt with isoglucose usage near saturation point, availability has been higher in recent years while there has been a pick up in consumption growth in Brazil after years of stagnation.

The proportion of total sugar production traded internationally has been falling for some years. From 34.67 percent in 1979/80 it fell to 31.09 in 1987/88 while this year it could be as low as 29.23 percent. This is particularly bad news for the white sugar exporters in view of the new refineries which are being established. Domestically refined sugar comes onto the Saudi Arabian market this month while several other refineries are under construction or on the drawing board in the Middle East.

Meanwhile Australia has expanded refining capacity while a third refinery is to be erected in Taiwan. For years white sugar took a steadily rising share of world trade; that tendency will now be sharply reversed.

Stocks are now forecast to reach 48 million tonnes at the end of August 1997. This is 40.21 percent of total demand compared with 39.82 percent last year. We had initially expected a stock rise to 42.27 percent but the lower figure reflects the drop in India, which because of the special circumstances which apply has little effect on the world market.

Much of the stability of world market prices in recent weeks was attributed to expectations of a lower crop in 1997/98 and another healthy rise in sugar offtake. A consumption figure of 123 million tonnes for 1997/98 should not be too far off the mark. Production is more difficult to assess as weather still has a crucial role to play but current indications are that production will not greatly change. If this assessment should prove to be correct, then taking into account unrecorded disappearance, a limited draw down of stocks seems to be on the cards.

Right now no earth shaking changes are on the horizon andwe may see another year of fairly stable prices with a slightly positive note. But it is still very early days and the market may not prove to be as dull as appears now.
